chapter: Arranging, Fletcher Henderson and Lucky Millinder
title: Playing with Lucky Millinder while waiting for his union card
summary: To make a living and satisfy the six-month union wait, he played and arranged for Millinder's showy band, which he left because it was not a jazz band.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Playing in Lionel Hampton's big band

blocks.x: Right, good. Well, let's get back to right where we are here. Well, you went out to the west coast and with Hawk, and then you were with Lucky Millinder for a while. I didn't realize that. Were you?
Yes. While I was in -- when I first went to New York, this is before this period that we're talking now, this is back when I first went to New York, when I joined Lester Young.
Yes.

Well, in order to earn a living, you know, very often, you know, there wasn't enough work on 52nd Street to keep me working all the time, and I was also putting in my time to join the musician's union. You were required to be in that area for a six month period. And I hadn't joined the union, so in order to join the union I played with Lucky Millinder, to, you know, make a living and put in my time.
I see.
You see.
Right, yes.

And I played with him and I wrote some arrangements for the band and he was kind enough to feature me in the band, when he had musical features. He was more or less an entertaining band which featured singers and high class arrangements. He had jazz arrangements of pieces like
you know, classical, some classical music, and Holiday in Strings was one of them.
Yes.

And he featured me on the piano, and these type of things. He was quite a showman, and he kept good musicians with him all the time. He had one of the best bands around New York, he was considered to be one of the top bands in New York, along with --
Who was in that band, can you remember?
Oh, there's plenty guys. Joe Guy was their trumpet player who later married Billie Holiday, you know about him. Oh, a lot of musicians played them. I could name quite a few of them.
Yes, Tab Smith, wasn't it?
Tab Smith.
Wasn't he in the band?

Yes, he was in the band, but not when I was in there. But he -- Lucky Millinder had the ability to pick musicians, and he tried to get all of the good musicians in his band with him. And he was a good guy to work for, and he was very, very congenial and very flattering to musicians. But I didn't stay with him too long because he wasn't a jazz player, and you know the band wasn't really my particular style, you know. But I stayed with the band --
Yeah. But it helped you through that
period.
Oh, sure, of course. It was a very good job for that time, you know.
